citation.claim: SEL can be organised as five interrelated competencies (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making), taught through sequenced, active, focused and explicit (SAFE) instruction in safe, caring, culturally responsive settings.
citation.source: CASEL, What is the CASEL Framework?

casel.checked: 2026-11-18; Read competency definitions, the SAFE description and the equity/culturally responsive statements. A framework description, not evidence that any authored activity works; CASEL itself notes SEL alone does not resolve structural inequity.

citation.claim: Primary SEL guidance recommends teaching skills explicitly and integrating/modelling them: expand emotion vocabulary with stories and games, teach 'I feel … because …' messages and that feelings are acceptable while some behaviours are not, teach self-calming, positive self-talk and body-cue awareness, use stories, hot seating and scenarios for perspective-taking, role-play communication and group skills, involve pupils in class rules, and teach a stepped problem-solving routine begun when children are calm.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation (2019), Improving Social and Emotional Learning in Primary Schools: Guidance Report, recommendations 1–2 and pp. 10–16.

eefSel.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the recommendation summary and the self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship-skill and decision-making strategy pages. Not adopted: the example of 'appropriate eye contact' as a listening criterion (neurodivergent learners), and the Box 3 task asking children to write about their own strong emotion (replaced with fictional scenarios). Programme-level evidence does not validate the authored activities.

citation.claim: By the end of primary, Relationships Education in England covers families that look different but are characterised by love and care; caring friendships that have ups and downs, include others and are worked through without violence; respectful relationships including boundaries, assertiveness versus being controlling, respecting difference, stereotypes and how to challenge them, bullying types and bystander responsibilities (primarily reporting to an adult), and seeking help.
citation.source: Department for Education (2025, in force 1 September 2026), Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education (RSE) and Health Education statutory guidance, primary Relationships Education content (pp. 8–9).

rshePrimaryRelationships.checked: 2026-11-18; Read primary 'Families and people who care for me', 'Caring friendships' and 'Respectful, kind relationships' content. Statutory for schools in England only; used as a content and safeguarding reference, not as a universal sequence or age threshold.

citation.claim: Primary Relationships Education covers respectful online interaction, risks from people who pretend online, harmful content/contact and reporting, caution about sharing information and images, boundaries, privacy and that it is not always right to keep secrets that relate to safety, that each person's body belongs to them, appropriate and unsafe contact, how to report abuse or concerns, and how to keep asking for help until heard.
citation.source: Department for Education (2025, in force 1 September 2026), RSHE statutory guidance, primary 'Online safety and awareness' and 'Being safe' content (p. 10).

rshePrimarySafety.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the primary online safety and being-safe content. England statutory guidance; schools elsewhere use their own safeguarding policy, reporting routes and legal frame.

citation.claim: Teaching sensitive topics can use distancing techniques, class ground rules and anonymous question boxes; staff should be trained in safeguarding because disclosures may increase, and should be clear that being a victim of abuse is never the child's fault.
citation.source: Department for Education (2025, in force 1 September 2026), RSHE statutory guidance, principles and paras 35–36.

rsheSensitive.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the delivery principles and paragraphs 35–36. The never-the-child's-fault statement appears in the secondary RSE paragraph; it is applied here as a safeguarding principle, not as a claim about primary statutory content.

citation.claim: Primary health education covers the range and scale of emotions, that worrying and feeling down are normal and not in themselves a mental health condition, varied vocabulary for own and others' feelings, judging whether feelings and behaviour are proportionate, loneliness, change and loss, where and how to seek support, critical evaluation of online information, sun safety, hygiene/handwashing, hazards, road and water safety, emergency calls, and correct names of body parts with personal boundaries.
citation.source: Department for Education (2025, in force 1 September 2026), RSHE statutory guidance, primary health and wellbeing content (pp. 21–25).

rshePrimaryHealth.checked: 2026-11-18; Read general wellbeing, wellbeing online, health protection, personal safety, first aid and developing bodies content. England statutory content; correct-term teaching and sequencing follow each school's policy and parental consultation arrangements.

citation.claim: Secondary content covers talking about emotions accurately, that ordinary worry is not itself a mental health condition and normal feelings should not be labelled as conditions, characteristics of common mental ill health presented carefully, unhealthy comparison and curated images online, misinformation and targeted advertising, that forwarding sexual images of under-18s is a crime and pupils will not be in trouble for seeking help, and that staff follow safeguarding procedures for disclosures.
citation.source: Department for Education (2025, in force 1 September 2026), RSHE statutory guidance, secondary online/media and health and wellbeing content (pp. 25–28).

rsheSecondary.checked: 2026-11-18; Read secondary online and media, mental wellbeing and wellbeing online items and paras 41–47. Used only for the age 12–14 topics; the image-law statement is England's legal frame and is not presented as universal law.

citation.claim: The Australian Curriculum Personal and Social capability organises learning into self-awareness (personal and emotional awareness, reflective practice), self-management (goal setting, emotional regulation, perseverance and adaptability), social awareness (empathy, relational and community awareness) and social management (communication, collaboration, leadership, decision-making, conflict resolution).
citation.source: Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, Australian Curriculum v9, Understand this general capability: Personal and Social capability.

acaraPsc.checked: 2026-11-18; Read element/sub-element structure. A capability framework, not teaching-efficacy evidence or a fixed age ladder.

citation.claim: The Australian Curriculum describes two distinct First Nations Peoples each encompassing many nations and peoples, sophisticated social organisation and kinship structures, languages with custodians, cultures that are not static, special connection to Country/Place, and occupation of the continent for more than 60,000 years.
citation.source: Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, Understand this cross-curriculum priority: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures.

acaraFirstNations.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the priority's organising ideas. The 'more than 60,000 years' figure is the curriculum's stated frame; archaeological dating estimates differ by site and method, so records qualify rather than treat one figure as settled. Local cultural authority is not supplied by this source.

citation.claim: Students who see bullying are advised to step in only if safe, support or accompany the person to get help, tell a trusted adult (privately if worried), not join in or laugh, not resend offensive messages or photos, and report online bullying to the platform and an adult.
citation.source: NSW Department of Education, Anti-bullying: I've seen someone bullied (student advice).

nswBystander.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the student advice. Jurisdiction-specific reporting routes (e.g. police, eSafety) are not generalised; children are not made responsible for confronting aggressors.

citation.claim: Australia's federal government handles matters such as defence, foreign affairs, immigration and currency; states and territories run services such as schools, hospitals, police and public transport; local councils look after local roads, waste, parks, pools and libraries, make by-laws and are funded by rates, charges and federal/state grants; education, health, environment and taxation are shared.
citation.source: Parliamentary Education Office, Three levels of government: governing Australia.

peoLevels.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the responsibility and funding lists and the shared-responsibility examples. The page does not state that councillors are elected; that fact is taken as a widely documented feature but not attributed to this source.

citation.claim: A federal bill must be passed in identical form by both the House of Representatives and the Senate and then receive Royal Assent from the Governor-General to become an Act of Parliament.
citation.source: Parliamentary Education Office, Law making.

peoLawMaking.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the law-making fact sheet. It describes laws as applying to everyone with legal consequences; it does not cover common law.

citation.claim: Australian law comes from statute law made by parliament, delegated law made under statute, and common law made by judges through precedent; statute law overrides common law.
citation.source: Parliamentary Education Office, Sources of law.

peoSourcesOfLaw.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full fact sheet (pitched at Year 8). Primary adaptations simplify delegated law away; the page does not define school/club rules.

citation.claim: Australia's system combines Westminster features (government formed in and responsible to an elected house, an opposition, a constitutional monarch acting on advice) with US-influenced features such as a Senate with equal state representation.
citation.source: Parliamentary Education Office, What is the Washminster system?

peoWashminster.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the answer. Details about the High Court's role are not attributed to this page.

citation.claim: Federal enrolment became compulsory in 1912 and voting at federal elections in 1924; electors mark their vote alone and in private in a voting compartment, with assistance available for some voters.
citation.source: Australian Electoral Commission, Electoral Backgrounder: Compulsory voting.

aecCompulsory.checked: 2026-11-18; Read dates and the private-voting description. Another AEC fact sheet dates compulsory enrolment to 1911; records avoid assessing that year. The 1856 colonial secret-ballot history was not verified on a fetched AEC page and is not used as an answer key.

citation.claim: The Torres Strait Islander flag, designed by the late Bernard Namok of Thursday Island, has green stripes for the land, black for the people and blue for the sea, a white dhari as a symbol of Torres Strait Islanders, and a white five-pointed star for peace, the five major island groups and navigation; it was proclaimed a Flag of Australia on 14 July 1995.
citation.source: Torres Strait Regional Authority, The Torres Strait flag.

tsraFlag.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the flag page. Flag reproduction rights are not addressed in the records; teachers use school-approved images.

citation.claim: Harold Thomas, a Luritja man, designed the Aboriginal flag: black represents Aboriginal people, yellow the sun, and red the earth and people's relationship to it (also ochre).
citation.source: Australian Museum, Indigenous Australia flags.

amFlags.checked: 2026-11-18; Read flag descriptions. The first-flown date differs across secondary sources (9 or 12 July 1971) and is not assessed.

citation.claim: Golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) was proclaimed Australia's national floral emblem on 1 September 1988, and 1 September was declared National Wattle Day in 1992.
citation.source: Australian National Botanic Gardens, Australia's national floral emblem.

anbgWattle.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the emblem history. The Coat of Arms description (shield of six state badges, kangaroo and emu supporters, seven-pointed star) could not be fetched from PM&C/APH (blocked); records keep it to the topic's own description and flag official-image checking.

citation.claim: First Nations, Inuit and Métis are three distinct Indigenous peoples in Canada with unique histories, languages, cultural practices and beliefs; more than 1.8 million people identified as Indigenous in the 2021 Census.
citation.source: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, Indigenous peoples and communities.

cirnac.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the overview. It does not list individual Nations or authorise any community's stories; creator identity must come from the book's own information.

citation.claim: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child sets out rights for every child without discrimination, including safety from violence, education, being heard, play and identity; the rights are universal and adults and governments must work so children can enjoy them.
citation.source: UNICEF UK, The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.

unicefUncrc.checked: 2026-11-18; Read summary of articles 2, 8, 12, 19, 28 and 31. The page does not make rights conditional on responsibilities; records therefore treat responsibilities as respecting others' rights, not as a price for having rights.

citation.claim: Positive, tolerable and toxic stress describe the body's response; brief positive stress is normal, tolerable stress is buffered by supportive adults, and toxic stress follows strong, frequent or prolonged adversity without supportive relationships.
citation.source: Center on the Developing Child, Harvard University, Toxic Stress (key concept).

harvardStress.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the three response types and buffering role of adults. This is not the eustress/distress terminology in the topic; records note the different framework rather than equating terms.

citation.claim: The brain continues maturing into the mid-to-late 20s, the prefrontal cortex (planning, prioritising, decisions) is among the last areas to mature, peer/social reward can weigh heavily in teen risk-taking, the teen brain is adaptable, many mental illnesses can first appear in adolescence, and teens may respond to stress differently.
citation.source: National Institute of Mental Health, The Teen Brain: 7 Things to Know.

nimhTeen.checked: 2026-11-18; Read all seven points. A public summary; it does not support deterministic claims that teens cannot decide well or that one brain region 'causes' an emotion.

citation.claim: In largely adult experimental and individual-difference research, reappraisal (changing how a situation is construed) often reduces emotional experience without memory cost, while expressive suppression reduces outward expression but not experience and can impair memory and raise physiological responding.
citation.source: Gross, J. J. (2002), Emotion regulation: Affective, cognitive, and social consequences, Psychophysiology 39, 281–291 (abstract).

grossRegulation.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the abstract and introduction. Adult laboratory evidence; it does not establish that all restraint of expression is harmful in every cultural context or that reappraisal suits every situation (e.g. genuine danger or injustice).

citation.claim: Two meta-analyses found weak overall relationships between growth mindset and achievement and weak effects of mindset interventions, with some support for possible benefits to students with low socioeconomic status or academic risk.
citation.source: Sisk, V. F., Burgoyne, A. P., Sun, J., Butler, J. L., & Macnamara, B. N. (2018), To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Psychological Science 29(4), 549–571.

siskMindset.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the abstract. Supports teaching the idea cautiously alongside strategies and feedback, not claiming that a mindset lesson raises attainment.

citation.claim: A conceptual replication of the marshmallow test with over 900 children found a small association between early delay and adolescent achievement that largely disappeared after accounting for family and early-environment characteristics.
citation.source: Association for Psychological Science, Observer: A new approach to the marshmallow test yields complex findings (on Watts, Duncan & Quan, 2018).

apsMarshmallow.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the summary. Used to avoid presenting waiting ability as a predictor of a child's future or as a virtue score.

citation.claim: Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence and relatedness as basic psychological needs and distinguishes intrinsic motivation from more or less internalised forms of extrinsic motivation; rewards and controls can affect intrinsic motivation.
citation.source: Center for Self-Determination Theory, The Theory.

sdt.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the theory overview. A theory-holder's own summary; no classroom effect size is inferred.

citation.claim: Procrastination can be understood as a self-regulation failure linked to short-term mood repair and emotion regulation, with costs borne by the future self.
citation.source: Sirois, F., & Pychyl, T. (2013), Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation: Consequences for future self, Social and Personality Psychology Compass 7(2), 115–127 (White Rose repository record).

siroisProcrastination.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the abstract. A review perspective, not proof that procrastination is never a planning, attention or workload issue; records say 'often' rather than 'only'.

citation.claim: In Lally and colleagues' study of a daily cued health behaviour, average time to peak automaticity was about 66 days with a wide range (18 to a predicted 254 days), and a single missed day had little effect.
citation.source: British Psychological Society Research Digest, How to form a habit (on Lally et al., 2010).

bpsHabit.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the digest. Adult volunteer sample; not a child norm, and the 'cue–routine–reward loop' wording in the topic is a popular model not attributed to this study.

citation.claim: Posttraumatic growth was described by Tedeschi and Calhoun in three broad themes (self-perception, relationships, philosophy of life) and measured with a five-factor inventory, but the factor structure has not replicated consistently.
citation.source: Osei-Bonsu, P. E., Weaver, T. L., Eisen, S. V., & Vander Wal, J. S. (2012), Posttraumatic Growth Inventory: Factor structure in the context of DSM-IV traumatic events, ISRN Psychiatry.

osseiPtg.checked: 2026-11-18; Read background, results and limitations (undergraduate convenience sample). Supports presenting growth as possible and contested, never expected or required of a person who has been harmed.

citation.claim: Virtue ethics emphasises virtues or moral character, in contrast to deontology's emphasis on duties or rules and consequentialism's emphasis on consequences; all three can accommodate virtues, rules and consequences in different roles.
citation.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Virtue Ethics (opening sections).

sepVirtue.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the opening characterisation and helping example. The three-way division is a teaching simplification; many ethical traditions (including religious and Indigenous ethics) fall outside it.

citation.claim: Effective altruism describes itself as using evidence and reasoning to find the best ways to do good, guided by principles such as scope sensitivity, impartiality and recognition of trade-offs, and says it does not endorse ends-justify-the-means reasoning.
citation.source: Centre for Effective Altruism, Introduction to effective altruism.

eaIntro.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the movement's self-description. A proponent source with limited engagement with critiques; records present it as one contested framework and never ask children to donate money.

citation.claim: Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced 'intersectionality' around 1989 to describe how race, gender and other forms of power interlock, so treating them separately can erase people's combined experience.
citation.source: Columbia Law School, Kimberlé Crenshaw on intersectionality, more than two decades later (2017).

crenshaw.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the interview. Not used to rank identities or to require any learner to describe their own identity or disadvantage.

citation.claim: In a survey of about 13,000 UK primary pupils aged 7–11 drawing their future jobs, gender stereotyping appeared early; family, TV, radio and film were the biggest influences and fewer than 1% knew of a job from a school visitor.
citation.source: Education and Employers, Drawing the Future report published (2018).

drawingFuture.checked: 2026-11-18; Read reported findings. Descriptive survey data, not causal evidence that a specific advert caused a choice.

citation.claim: The gender pay gap is the difference in pay between women and men across the workforce and is not the same as equal pay for the same or comparable work (a legal requirement in Australia since 1969); drivers include bias, industry and occupational segregation, part-time work, caring time out and unpaid work.
citation.source: Workplace Gender Equality Agency, The gender pay gap.

wgea.checked: 2026-11-18; Read definition, equal-pay distinction and drivers. No current percentage is used because the page did not state one; teachers supply a dated official figure.

citation.claim: The double empathy problem describes misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic people as a two-way breakdown in reciprocity rather than a deficit located only in autistic people; non-autistic people can misread autistic people's emotions.
citation.source: National Autistic Society, The double empathy problem (on Milton, 2012).

nasDoubleEmpathy.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the article. It does not itself give eye-contact guidance; records independently avoid scoring eye contact, facial display or stillness as evidence of empathy or listening.

citation.claim: A Grades 5–6 media-literacy lesson teaches pupils to analyse advertisement structure, differentiate information from selling, recognise codes of different ad categories, distinguish fantasy from reality and identify target audiences.
citation.source: MediaSmarts (2012), Advertising All Around Us, lesson plan for Grades 5–6.

mediaSmartsAds.checked: 2026-11-18; Read objectives and Key Concept 1–2 activities. Lesson design reference, not efficacy evidence; health-campaign comparison is an authored extension.

citation.claim: A study compared how professional fact-checkers, historians and first-year university students evaluated online information, and described fact-checkers' strategies (lateral reading) for efficiently finding trustworthy information.
citation.source: Wineburg, S., & McGrew, S. (2018), Lateral reading and the nature of expertise: Reading less and learning more when evaluating digital information, Stanford Digital Repository.

wineburgLateral.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the repository record and abstract only. Detailed group results are not attributed beyond the abstract; adult/university sample, so primary use is an adaptation.

citation.claim: Ontario's public guidance describes bullying as behaviour that makes the person bullied feel afraid or uncomfortable, which can be unwanted repeated aggression or happen one time, by one person or a group, often where there are real or perceived power imbalances; it lists forms including physical, verbal, social and cyber-bullying, and advises students to walk away, tell an adult they trust, report (including anonymously) through their school or board, and talk to others so they do not feel alone.
citation.source: Government of Ontario, Bullying: we can all help stop it.

ontarioBullying.checked: 2026-11-18; WebFetch was refused (HTTP 403), so the page was downloaded directly and its text read: 'About bullying', 'Types of bullying' and the student/witness advice sections. The page's helpline number and prevalence statistic are not used. 'Stay calm' in its student advice is not turned into a precondition for receiving help.

citation.claim: Ontario Policy/Program Memorandum 144 (issued 25 November 2021) states that bullying can be repeated or occur one time, can occur where there are real or perceived power imbalances, and cites the Education Act definition: aggressive and typically repeated behaviour that is intended, or that the pupil ought to know would be likely, to cause harm, fear or distress, in a context of real or perceived power imbalance, by physical, verbal, electronic, written or other means.
citation.source: Ontario Ministry of Education, Policy/Program Memorandum 144: Bullying prevention and intervention (2021).

ontarioPpm144.checked: 2026-11-18; WebFetch was refused (HTTP 403), so the memorandum was downloaded directly and its 'Understanding bullying and cyber-bullying' section and Education Act definition footnote read. Board procedural requirements are not summarised; Ontario is presented as one declared frame, not a universal definition.

citation.claim: Australia's national school definition describes bullying through three elements: a real or perceived imbalance of power, repetition or potential repetition (sharing hurtful content online even once can count because it can be shared and repeated), and intentional acts that are aggressive, negative or harmful; it can be verbal, physical, social, in person or online, overt or covert. Single incidents and conflicts between equals are not defined as bullying, but unkind actions can hurt and should be addressed.
citation.source: Australian Government, Bullying. No Way!, What is bullying?

bullyingNoWay.checked: 2026-11-18; Re-fetched and read the definition, elements and one-off/online notes. Presented as the Australian national school frame, not a universal definition.

citation.claim: The Australian definition resource summarises the three main features of bullying (power imbalance, actual or potential repetition, intentional harmful acts), says single incidents and disagreements between equals are not bullying, and states that it is important for schools to respond to any inappropriate behaviour and ensure every person feels safe.
citation.source: Australian Government, Bullying. No Way!, The definition of bullying (resource).

bnwDefinition.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the three-feature summary and the statements about single incidents, equal conflicts, online sharing and responding to any inappropriate behaviour. The full verbatim definition is not reproduced on this page.
